Not 100 because C5 has neither route available here: zig rejects nothing and its ThreadSanitizer cannot run on this host. Not Adequate (60) because C1, C2, C3 and C6 are each independently evidenced from the published std source and the langref, cross-checked against the installed toolchain.

cross_language_consistency_note: One rubric, six binary indicators, applied in the frozen evidence_collection_order (Python, C++, Rust, Go, Java, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, Zig, Quidra LAST); the level is the mechanical count, with no holistic step. C1: the identical frozen workload (N=500000000, 4 fixed chunks, chunk c handled by worker w where c%W==w so the combination order is the same at W=1 and W=4), built with each language's frozen conc1_build_and_run recipe, 5 runs at 1 worker and 5 at 4 workers, median compared against median/1.5 on this 8-logical-CPU host. Nine languages printed the bit-identical value 249999999.8718209565 (Java and Kotlin print 249999999.8718209600 because they accumulate in the same order but format from the JVM's double formatter; each was compared against itself at W=1 vs W=4, which is what the indicator asks). Quidra's probe was written to the same specification with the mechanism CONC-1.worker_model admits for it, and was measured, not presumed. C2 is conjunctive and was scored with no_partial_credit: Python fails on atomics only, TypeScript fails on all three at the version under test, and no language was given the indicator for two out of three. C3 was applied with one rule fixed before any language was scored and applied to all ten: the type must transfer a SEQUENCE of values between concurrent workers, which is what 'channel, queue, mailbox' denote. That admitted queue.Queue, mpsc, Go channels, BlockingQueue, MessagePort, Kotlin Channel, AsyncStream and std.Io.Queue, and excluded C++'s one-shot promise/future (C++ has no channel type at all: 'channel' occurs zero times in the C++ working draft). C4 counts a model provided by the language OR its first-party standard library and usable without a third-party package; a hand-written driver is not a third-party package, so Rust's async/await and C++'s coroutines qualify on the same footing as asyncio, goroutines, virtual threads, Kotlin coroutines, Swift tasks and std.Io.async. C5 was executed for all ten with the same two admitted routes, in the same order: (1) does the toolchain REJECT the frozen CONC-2 probe at compile time with a diagnostic naming the unsynchronized shared access, and (2) does a race detector shipped with the toolchain or published by the official_project_set report it when run. Only Rust (route 1) and Go (route 2) passed. Swift's Swift-6/strict-concurrency diagnostics name the access but are warnings that still produce a binary, so they are route-1 failures, and the same warning-is-not-rejection line was applied to every language. ThreadSanitizer is admissible for C++, Swift and Zig and builds for all three, but every TSan binary on this host segfaults (verified down to a hello world, and verified identically with the tool sandbox disabled), so all three lose C5 for the same recorded reason, state S4. C6 required a named first-party abstraction ABOVE raw threads; documentation telling the reader to implement one (Node.js: 'When implementing a worker pool, use the AsyncResource API') was not accepted for any language. Cross-check of the ten assignments together: the three 80s (Java, Kotlin, Swift) and Zig all fail exactly C5 and nothing else; the two 100s (Rust, Go) differ from them only by having a working race check, and are reported at equal rank per tie_handling; the two 60s (Python, C++) each fail exactly two indicators; TypeScript at 40 fails three; Quidra at 0 fails all six. No two languages with the same satisfied set received different levels, and no two with different satisfied sets received the same level by accident rather than by count.
limitations: C5 for C++, Swift and Zig is verification_status=unverified / availability_state S4: ThreadSanitizer compiles for all three but no TSan-instrumented binary runs on macOS 26.4.1 arm64 (exit 139 even for a 4-line hello world, inside and outside the tool sandbox). The frozen rule states explicitly that S4 does not rescue an indicator requiring execution, so all three are scored NOT SATISFIED; this belongs in host_limited_indicators.json. Had TSan run, C++ would plausibly be 80, and Swift and Zig 100.

rubric_verification_recipes freezes a conc1_build_and_run command per language but freezes NO command for CONC-2. The C5 check was therefore defined at scoring time and applied uniformly: compile with the frozen build recipe, then, where the language documents a stricter data-race checking mode or ships/names a race detector, run that too. The exact commands for all ten are in standard/rubrics/logs/conc2_c5.log.

The Quidra CONC-1 probe (probes/CONC-1/quidra/conc1.qui) and the Quidra CONC-2 probe (probes/CONC-2/quidra/conc2.qui) did not exist when this metric was resumed and were written for this run, after all nine other languages' CONC-1 timings had already been recorded (2026-09-18T20:35Z-20:48Z) and after their C5 checks. That ordering satisfies evidence_collection_order; it also means the Quidra probes were not reviewed by a second party, unlike the nine that were built earlier.

Quidra's CONC-1 probe hard-codes its own executable path as the default of a --self option ('./build/conc1-quidra') because quidra 0.2.0's cli binding exposes no argv[0]. The frozen recipe's command lines ('./build/conc1-quidra 1' and '... 4') run unchanged.

A /bin/sh-mediated variant (process.run('/bin/sh', ['-c', 'worker0 & worker1 & ... wait'])) would give Quidra real parallel speedup. It was NOT measured or counted, because CONC-1.worker_model requires a mechanism 'provided by the language itself or by its first-party standard library' and the concurrency there is supplied by the shell's job control, not by Quidra. No other language was permitted to shell out either. This is recorded so the exclusion is visible rather than silent.

Rust's std documentation was served at version 1.98.1 (released 2026-09-01) while the toolchain under test is rustc 1.95.0; E2 admits 'the toolchain version under test or the nearest published version'. Every API cited (Mutex, Condvar, atomic, mpsc, thread::scope, async/await) predates 1.95.0.

For C++ the frozen official_docs_root list does not include a browsable standard-library reference. C2/C3/C4/C6 were therefore taken from N5054, the C++ Working Draft published at open-std.org, which IS a frozen official_docs_root. Text was extracted from the PDF locally; clause numbers are given so any reader can check the quotes.

Zig's standard-library reference at ziglang.org/documentation/0.16.0/std/ is a WASM application that serves the documented source as sources.tar. The doc comments quoted were read from that published tarball and cross-checked line-for-line against the installed toolchain's std. No rendered HTML page carries these sentences.

All documentation pages were accessed on 2026-09-19, after the 2026-09-17 evidence cutoff, but every cited artifact is dated on or before the cutoff (N5054 2026-07-16, Java SE 26 2026-04-21, Rust 1.98.1 2026-09-01, node v24.2.0, zig 0.16.0, Kotlin docs 2026-09-01). This treatment is identical for all ten languages. Accession timestamps are recorded to the minute from the fetch logs.

Kotlin's C2 and C3 rely on kotlinx.coroutines and, for the condition-variable conjunct, on JetBrains' and OpenJDK's documented primitives. Both publishers are in Kotlin's frozen official_project_set, and all excerpts are from kotlinlang.org, Kotlin's own official_docs_root; a narrower reading that restricted 'first-party standard library' to kotlin-stdlib alone would cost Kotlin C3 and move it to 60.

TypeScript's C2 was scored against the Node.js v24.2.0 documentation because v24.2.0 is the runtime under test. Node v24.5.0 adds worker_threads.locks (a mutual-exclusion primitive, Stability 1 - Experimental); even counting it, C2 still fails on the condition-variable and atomics conjuncts, so the level does not change.
